entities.name: Jacques Bongars
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jacques Bongars (died 1612-06-29) was a prominent French scholar, diplomat, and polymath active during the late 16th and early 17th centuries. Operating amidst the aftermath of the French Wars of Religion and the consolidation of Bourbon power under Henry IV, Bongars distinguished himself through extensive diplomatic service across Europe and his monumental contributions to historical scholarship, particularly in philology and the study of the Crusades. His work represents a crucial bridge between Renaissance humanism and early modern historical methodology, emphasizing critical textual recovery and dissemination.

As a diplomat, Bongars served as a trusted envoy for Henry IV, undertaking sensitive missions to various German states, Switzerland, and Italy. These assignments aimed to secure French political interests, foster Protestant alliances against Habsburg influence, and negotiate complex international relations following the Edict of Nantes. Concurrently, his scholarly pursuits culminated in the 1611 publication of *Gesta Dei per Francos*, a two-volume compendium of 39 medieval Latin chronicles detailing the First Crusade and the Latin East. This meticulous editorial project brought together seminal works by authors such as William of Tyre, Albert of Aix, and Fulcher of Chartres, many of which were previously obscure or inaccessible.

Bongars's *Gesta Dei per Francos* profoundly shaped the study of the Crusades for over two centuries, becoming the foundational and most comprehensive collection of primary sources available to scholars. It served as the indispensable reference for generations of historians, influencing narratives and research until the advent of more extensive critical editions in the 19th century. His diplomatic efforts, meanwhile, contributed significantly to the stabilization of post-Wars of Religion France and the establishment of its alliances within the intricate European political landscape.
